strengths: Innovative dataset generation: The evolutionary construction of a diverse synthetic chaotic ODE dataset (2 x 10^4 systems) utilizing mutation, skew-product recombination, and strict chaoticity filters (like the 0-1 test and Lyapunov exponent estimation).

Strong grounding in dynamical systems theory: The model architecture incorporates key concepts like Takens' embedding theorem (via patching) and Koopman operator theory (via polynomial and Fourier feature embeddings).

Outstanding empirical results: Panda demonstrates impressive zero-shot forecasting performance across diverse real-world systems (double pendulum, C. elegans, electronic circuits) and even high-dimensional PDEs, outperforming general time-series foundation models.

Insightful scaling law and interpretability: The paper identifies a unique scaling law based on dynamical system diversity rather than just data volume, and provides a compelling interpretability analysis showing nonlinear resonance patterns in the attention maps.
weaknesses: The handling of varying channel dimensions is slightly underspecified in the main text. While Section B explains that 3 channels are randomly sampled during training to enable batching and that channel attention treats channels as a set, a more detailed explanation of how the model generalizes from 3 channels to high-dimensional systems (such as the 28-channel electronic circuit or the 64-channel PDE) at inference time would enhance clarity.

The ablation study shows that Masked Language Modeling (MLM) pretraining improves short-term forecasting but degrades autoregressive rollout performance. Although acknowledged as a limitation, the underlying reason for this trade-off is not fully explained or resolved.
Visual clarity of some figures (e.g., Figure 2, 4, and 5) could be improved, as axis labels, legends, and text are quite small and difficult to read.

strengths: A highly novel and rigorous dataset generation pipeline: using an evolutionary search algorithm (mutation, skew-product recombination, and chaoticity filtering) to create 20,000 unique chaotic ODE systems is a major contribution that addresses the data scarcity bottleneck in scientific machine learning (SciML).

Strong theoretical grounding: the architecture explicitly integrates inductive biases from dynamical systems theory, including Koopman operator-inspired embeddings (random polynomial and Fourier features) and decoupled temporal and channel attention to handle spatial-temporal coupling and Takens' embedding theorem.

Remarkable out-of-distribution zero-shot generalization: the model's ability to zero-shot forecast complex real-world experimental systems (Double Pendulum, Eigenworms, Electronic Circuits) and even high-dimensional chaotic PDEs (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, von Kármán vortex street) is exceptionally impressive.

Insightful analysis of representations: the exploration of 'nonlinear resonance' inside the attention heads via frequency sweep analysis, alongside the identification of a distinct neural scaling law relating performance to dynamical diversity rather than just raw dataset size, adds great scientific value to the paper.
High-quality writing, excellent schematic diagrams, and thorough appendices making the work highly readable.
weaknesses: Details on higher-dimensional testing are slightly sparse: during training, the model is restricted to 3-dimensional inputs for batching. However, during testing, it is evaluated on systems with higher dimensions (e.g., PDEs discretized into many spatial coordinates acting as channels). The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of how the channel attention mechanism handles this sudden expansion in the number of channels (e.g., from 3 to 64+) during zero-shot testing.

A trade-off with Masked Language Modeling (MLM): Figure 3 shows that MLM pretraining actually degrades long-term autoregressive rollout performance despite improving short-term predictions. The authors acknowledge this limitation, but a deeper discussion on why MLM breaks trajectory continuity or attractor-geometry learning would strengthen the paper.

The baseline comparison is limited to general-purpose time series foundation models (Chronos, TimesFM, TimeMoE). Comparing against existing specialized physics-informed or neural operator baselines (even if trained in a few-shot or in-distribution setting) would highlight Panda's unique advantages more prominently.

strengths: The paper is exceptionally well-grounded in dynamical systems theory. The authors elegantly justify their architectural choices (e.g., patching via Takens' embedding theorem, dynamics embedding via Koopman operator/eDMD theory, and channel attention to address multivariate coupling) using physical and mathematical principles.

The evolutionary framework used to generate the dataset of 20,000 chaotic ODEs is highly creative and rigorous. Employing strict chaoticity filters (0-1 test, power spectrum tests, and Lyapunov exponent estimation) ensures a high-quality, mathematically sound dataset that is a valuable contribution in itself.

The empirical results are highly compelling. Panda demonstrates strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities on unseen synthetic systems, real-world experimental benchmarks (double pendulum, eigenworms, circuits), and even generalizes zero-shot to complex, high-dimensional PDEs (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, von Kármán vortex street) without retraining.

The analysis of the model's inner workings is outstanding. Probing the attention maps using two-tone sinusoids to demonstrate nonlinear resonance is a brilliant and physically meaningful diagnostic tool. Additionally, establishing a scaling law with respect to the diversity of dynamical systems (rather than just raw data volume) provides important insights for foundation models in scientific ML.
weaknesses: The polynomial feature construction in the Dynamics Embedding (similar to extended DMD) may face scalability issues as the number of channels $C$ increases. While the paper circumvents this by sampling 3 channels during training, a more detailed discussion of the computational complexity and scaling limits of these features would be beneficial.

For the PDE evaluation section, comparing solely against general time-series models (Chronos, TimesFM) leaves a small gap. Comparing Panda's zero-shot performance against established neural operators (e.g., Fourier Neural Operators) or classical spatiotemporal forecasting baselines would further highlight its competitiveness.

The authors observe that Masked Language Model (MLM) pretraining degrades autoregressive rollout performance but improves single-step completions. A deeper investigation or discussion into why this performance trade-off occurs in dynamical systems forecasting would strengthen the paper's conclusions.

strengths: Highly innovative dataset generation: The paper presents an evolutionary framework using skew-product coupling to generate a massive, diverse, and rigorously verified dataset of over 20,000 chaotic dynamical systems. The filtering pipeline (using the 0-1 chaos test, Lyapunov exponent estimation, and stationarity tests) ensures high-quality training trajectories.

Dynamics-informed architecture design: The components of Panda are carefully motivated by dynamical systems theory. The use of patching is linked to Takens' embedding theorem, the polynomial and Fourier embeddings are connected to Koopman operator theory (eDMD), and the cross-channel attention effectively models multivariate coupling, which is typically ignored by univariate foundation models.

Impressive emergent zero-shot generalization: Despite being trained entirely on low-dimensional (d=3) synthetic ODEs, the model exhibits strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities on real-world experimental systems (e.g., C. Elegans posture, double pendulum, electronic circuits) and, crucially, high-dimensional chaotic PDEs (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and von Kármán vortex street).

Deep theoretical insights and scaling laws: The paper introduces a novel dynamical systems scaling law, showing that zero-shot forecasting error scales with the number of unique training dynamical systems rather than simply the number of trajectories/initial conditions on a few systems. This is beautifully motivated by ergodic theory (Pesin's theorem).

Thorough evaluation and excellent execution: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written with high-quality visualizations of attractors, robust statistical significance tests, extensive ablation studies, and insightful attention map analysis (e.g., demonstrating nonlinear resonance).
weaknesses: Autoregressive rollout decay: As noted in Section 5.4, when Panda is rolled out autoregressively far beyond its training horizon, it tends to regress to the mean. While it still outperforms baselines on distributional metrics, resolving or mitigating this mean-regression remains an open challenge for long-term climate/attractor emulation.

Fixed-dimension training constraint: To batch trajectories of mixed dimensionalities, the training is constrained by randomly sampling 3 channels from each trajectory. While this works surprisingly well and generalizes, it may prevent the model from learning more complex, higher-order joint interactions during the pretraining stage.

strengths: The paper is exceptionally well-grounded in dynamical systems theory. The architectural choices, such as patching and embedding with polynomial/Fourier features, are carefully motivated by mathematical concepts like Takens' embedding theorem and extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition (eDMD).

The proposed dataset generation pipeline is highly innovative. Using an evolutionary algorithm to mutate and recombine a base set of chaotic systems, while filtering candidates with rigorous mathematical criteria (e.g., Lyapunov exponents, 0-1 chaos test, near-recurrence tests), provides a high-quality, diverse dataset of chaotic trajectories.

The empirical results are outstanding. PANDA outperforms robust univariate and multivariate time-series baselines (including Chronos and TimesFM) in zero-shot forecasting on both synthetic chaotic datasets and real-world physical systems (such as C. elegans posture and electronic circuits).

The zero-shot PDE forecasting results are an impressive showcase of emergent capability. Predicting complex phenomena like flame front merging in Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and vortex pinchoff in VKVS without having seen PDEs during training is a striking result.

The manuscript is extremely thorough, featuring a detailed analysis of attention maps (revealing nonlinear resonance), mathematical proofs of implicit spatio-temporal coupling, and insightful scaling laws showing that system diversity is the key driver of generalization.
weaknesses: Although PANDA excels at short-to-medium-term forecasting, it eventually suffers from regression to the mean on long-term rollouts (as noted in Figure 30). This limit on long-term rollout remains an open challenge compared to models that sustain long-term variance through other means (like 'parroting').

For the PDE evaluation in Section 5.5, the comparison is only made against time-series foundation models (Chronos, TimesFM). It would enrich the evaluation to compare PANDA's zero-shot performance against established neural operators (e.g., Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) or DeepONets) trained in a supervised manner, to benchmark the performance gap between zero-shot generalization and in-domain training.

During training, the multivariate trajectories are constrained to 3 dimensions by randomly sampling 3 channels to facilitate batching. While computationally convenient, this step might restrict the model's ability to natively capture complex, highly coordinated high-dimensional patterns during pretraining.

strengths: Novel Dataset Generation Framework: The paper presents a creative evolutionary algorithm to generate a large-scale, diverse dataset of chaotic ODEs (~20,000 systems) starting from 129 base systems. The use of strict mathematical filters (0-1 chaos test, Lyapunov exponent estimation, stationarity tests) ensures high-quality chaotic trajectories.

Interesting Scaling Law Analysis: The study of how data diversity (number of unique systems vs. number of initial conditions) impacts generalization under a fixed total token budget is insightful and highly relevant for pretraining in scientific machine learning.

Diverse Evaluation Scenarios: The authors test the model on multiple challenging setups, including synthetic held-out ODEs, real-world experimental systems (e.g., C. Elegans, double pendulum, electronic circuits), and high-dimensional PDEs.

Analysis of Model Inner Workings: The paper provides valuable qualitative analyses of the learned attention maps, illustrating phenomena like nonlinear resonance and implicit spatio-temporal coupling.
weaknesses: Unfair Baseline Comparison (Multivariate vs. Univariate): The primary baselines compared in the paper (Chronos, TimesFM, Time-MoE) are univariate time series models. In chaotic dynamical systems, the state variables are highly coupled. A univariate model is forced to forecast each channel independently, which is a massive disadvantage because it lacks access to the simultaneous states of the other variables. To demonstrate the true value of Panda, it must be compared against standard multivariate forecasting baselines (e.g., multivariate PatchTST, Vector Autoregression, multivariate LSTMs/GRUs).

Weak Evaluation on PDEs: The claim of 'emergent PDE forecasting capability' is overhyped. The PDEs (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and von Kármán vortex street) are reduced to 64 Fourier or PCA modes, which are then treated as a 64-dimensional multivariate trajectory. The baselines for this task are again limited to Chronos (univariate). There is no comparison to standard PDE surrogate models (e.g., Fourier Neural Operators (FNO), DeepONet) or even simple linear autoregressive models (like DMD).

Limited Recombination Diversity: The evolutionary recombination scheme relies on asymmetric master-slave coupling. While this mathematically guarantees the preservation of chaoticity, it produces a very specific class of coupled systems where one subsystem is completely independent of the other. It is unclear if a model trained on such asymmetric structures generalizes well to fully coupled symmetric systems.

Inconsistent Ablation Results: In Figure 3, the combination of MLM pretraining and the proposed dynamics embedding actually decreases performance compared to using them individually. This interaction is not well-understood or resolved, and the overall performance margins between several ablated variants are small and overlapping.

Channel Scaling at Inference: The model is trained on fixed 3-dimensional trajectories. However, during inference, it is applied to higher-dimensional systems (up to 64 channels for PDEs). The paper does not sufficiently explain how the cross-channel attention mechanism, trained only on 3 channels, scales to 64 channels without experiencing distribution shift or representation collapse.

strengths: Novel and theoretically-grounded data generation: The evolutionary search algorithm leveraging skew-product coupling to generate 20k chaotic ODEs represents a major step forward for scientific machine learning (SciML) training data, moving beyond simple parameter-jittering of a few base systems.

Strong theoretical integration: The architecture cleverly integrates inductive biases from dynamical systems theory, such as Takens' embedding theorem motivating the patching strategy, and Koopman/eDMD operator theory motivating the polynomial and Fourier dynamics embeddings.

Thorough and diverse evaluation: The evaluation is highly comprehensive, covering a massive synthetic test set, real-world physical systems (EigenWorms, Double Pendulum, circuits), and complex chaotic PDEs (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, von Kármán vortex street), demonstrating remarkable zero-shot generalization.

Scaling Law with Diversity: The discovery of a scaling law based on dynamical system diversity (while holding total training points constant) is a highly significant insight that bridges learning complexity with attractor topology and Pesin's theorem.
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is beautifully illustrated, clear, incredibly thorough (45 pages of deep analysis in the appendix), and provides code/model checkpoints.
weaknesses: Degradation of rollout performance via MLM: As noted by the authors, MLM pretraining improves completion tasks but degrades autoregressive rollout. The paper would benefit from a deeper exploration of why this trade-off occurs.

Limited scaling of parameters: Although the authors explore up to 72M parameters, it remains relatively small compared to modern massive time-series foundation models. A brief discussion on whether further scaling shows diminishing returns or if there are computational bottlenecks with the patch/channel-attention scheme would be useful.

Explanation of emergent PDE forecasting: The mechanism behind the emergent ability to forecast spatial PDEs (e.g., how the model handles discretized spatial fields mapped as multivariate channels) is intriguing but could be discussed with more mathematical or structural depth in the main text.

strengths: Intriguing and Relevant Research Topic: Focusing on pretraining global foundation models specifically tailored for chaotic dynamical systems (SciML) rather than general, unstructured time-series data is a highly promising and timely research direction.

Rigorous Dataset Construction Pipeline: The evolutionary search framework uses a thorough suite of attractor tests (such as the chaos 0-1 test, near-recurrence tests, power spectrum analysis, and the Rosenstein estimator for Lyapunov exponents) to ensure the generated synthetic data represents true chaotic trajectories.

Evaluation on Real-World Experimental Data: The paper evaluates the model on actual experimental physical datasets (Double Pendulum, EigenWorms, and Electronic Circuits), demonstrating that pretraining on simulated ODEs can translate to real-world physical systems.

Extensive Supplementary Material: The appendix provides a large volume of additional material, including qualitative forecasting examples, model configurations, and detailed derivations of implicit spatio-temporal coupling in the transformer layers.
weaknesses: Weak and Unfair Baseline Comparisons: For multivariate chaotic forecasting, the model is primarily compared against univariate time-series foundation models (Chronos, TimesFM, TimeMoE). Since these models forecast each dimension independently, they are fundamentally unable to capture the coupled multivariate attractor geometry. Comparing a multivariate model to univariate baselines on highly coupled systems is a weak baseline setup; a standard multivariate transformer or MLP trained on the same data should have been included. Additionally, for the PDE experiments (Figure 6), comparing Panda to FNO and DeepONet 'fully-trained on the context' (which means training on a single sequence of length 512) is highly unfair. Operator learning models like FNO are designed to learn mappings between function spaces using thousands of trajectories, and training them from scratch on a single context window is guaranteed to yield extremely poor results.

Channel-Permutation Invariance vs. Spatial PDE Structure: The multivariate channel attention layer does not use positional encodings across the channel dimension to allow generalization to arbitrary channel sizes. However, this permutation-invariant structure means the model treats the channels as an unstructured bag of variables. For PDEs (such as Kuramoto-Sivashinsky), spatial structure and local derivatives (e.g., spatial proximity) are fundamental. The paper does not thoroughly address how a permutation-invariant channel mixer can physically model spatial derivative structures.

Limitations of the Evolutionary Dataset Diversity: The evolutionary recombination relies on a simple asymmetric master-slave (skew-product) coupling where the driver system unidirectionally forces the response system. Under such unidirectional coupling, response systems often undergo generalized synchronization to the driver. Consequently, many of the 20,000 'discovered' systems might just be synchronized variations of the same 129 parent attractors, rather than topologically novel chaotic systems, limiting the true physical diversity of the dataset.

Overclaiming and Grandiose Terminology: The paper frequently uses highly hyped language (e.g., 'spontaneously develops the ability', 'emergent properties', 'dynamical systems scaling law'). The 'scaling law' in Figure 5 demonstrates a basic trade-off between unique systems and initial conditions with a very narrow range of performance improvement (sMAPE from ~45% to ~30%), making the designation of a 'dynamical systems scaling law' feel exaggerated. Moreover, the 'emergent' PDE forecasting capability is largely a structural consequence of using channel-permutation invariance rather than a spontaneous conceptual generalization by the model.

strengths: Highly novel and rigorous dataset generation methodology using an evolutionary algorithm to discover 20,000 chaotic ODEs, properly filtered using dynamical systems criteria (Lyapunov exponents, 0-1 test for chaos, near-recurrence). This addresses a major data scarcity bottleneck in scientific machine learning.

Elegant integration of dynamical systems theory into neural architecture design, including Koopman-motivated polynomial/Fourier patch embedding, Takens' delay embedding-motivated patching, and interleaved channel-temporal attention to handle strong coupling.

Comprehensive and highly impressive evaluations spanning out-of-domain synthetic chaotic systems, real-world physical experiments (Double Pendulum, EigenWorms, Electronic Circuits), and zero-shot transfer to complex, weakly-turbulent partial differential equations (PDEs) like Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Von Karman vortex streets.

Discovery of a unique 'dynamical systems scaling law' demonstrating that zero-shot forecast accuracy scales with the diversity of unique dynamical systems rather than just the number of training timepoints.

Fascinating analysis of learned representations (e.g., attention maps showing nonlinear resonance and recurrence structures), bridging the gap between neural network interpretability and classical physics.
weaknesses: The explanation of how the model handles variable numbers of input channels during inference is somewhat sparse in the main text. While Appendix B mentions subsampling 3 channels during training for efficient batching and processing full trajectories during inference, more mathematical details on how the channel attention maps scale to arbitrary dimensions at test time should be emphasized.

At very long prediction horizons, the model eventually suffers from mean regression (as discussed in Section 5.6), which is a common limitation of MSE-trained encoder-only architectures. In contrast, models like Chronos (probabilistic/tokenized) or DynaMix (recurrent) seem to preserve the long-term attractor geometry better in certain metrics (like geometric misalignment KL divergence in Table 15).

The evolutionary search and training are constrained to low-dimensional ODEs ($d=3$). Although the model demonstrates impressive zero-shot generalization to PDEs, scaling dense channel attention to very high-dimensional systems (e.g., atmospheric modeling with thousands of coupled variables) may present computational bottlenecks.
